growth_story.headline: Bulgaria's income per person shrank in the 1990s, boomed after a 1997 currency board, then grew more slowly but steadily as its population fell.
growth_story.arc: Income per person shrank by 2.8 percent a year in 1990–1999, a decade that ended in bank failures and hyperinflation in 1996–97; income per person fell 13.6 percent in 1997 alone. A currency board set up in July 1997 began a long run of tight budgets and low public debt, and from 2000 to 2008 income per person grew 6.9 percent a year, in a boom that sources tie to large capital inflows and the pull of joining the EU. When those inflows contracted, income per person fell 2.7 percent in 2009, and from 2009 to 2025 growth averaged 2.9 percent a year, with a fall of 2.2 percent in 2020 and a rebound of 8.5 percent in 2021. Over 2016–2025 growth averaged 3.7 percent a year, up from 3.4 in 2006–2015, and income per person reached a new high in 2025. Sources say recent growth has rested on strong domestic demand, fast wage gains and looser budgets, while productivity growth has lagged, the population keeps shrinking and the catch-up with EU incomes has been slower than in many regional peers.

threads.title: The crises of the 1990s
threads.text: Income per person fell every year from 1990 to 1993. In 1996 the weakest banks were closed, and in early 1997 hyperinflation struck, making 1997 the worst year in the data. The EBRD traces Bulgaria's lingering gap with its regional peers mainly to the crises of the 1990s.

threads.title: A shrinking population
threads.text: Bulgaria's population has fallen steadily since 1989, and its working-age population is expected to keep shrinking. Fewer people means income per person can rise even when total output grows slowly, and sources see the pressure from ageing growing stronger.

since_last_year.text: Bulgaria adopted the euro in January 2026. Growth held up through 2025 and early 2026 on strong domestic demand, despite political instability and weak exports. A wider budget deficit led the EU to open an Excessive Deficit Procedure, and an energy price shock linked to conflict in the Middle East pushed inflation up in spring 2026.

growth_story.tension: The sources stress that Bulgaria's catch-up has lagged many regional peers and that productivity growth is weak. The data look stronger: income per person grew 3.7 percent a year over 2016–2025, ranked 3 of 11 among structural peers, and reached a new high in 2025. Part of the gap is the shrinking population: the EBRD's average for total output growth since 2015 is well below the data's growth in income per person, because output is shared among fewer people each year. The sources and the data also compare Bulgaria with different groups of countries.
